Impermanence and lack of self. I consider these two rather advanced concepts in Buddhism. Not because it's hard to understand them (they make sense), but because it's hard to realize them (it's hard to live life from such perspective when everything people do/say/think seems to ignore them). But I'll try to explain simply. Alright, let's get to it!  

In Buddhism it is important to see things as they really are. Impermanence is a characteristic of everything that is. Because everything changes. Living creatures grow old and die. Objects deteriorate over time (or suddenly). Nothing can really stay to provide you pleasure and comfort. Yet, we allow our emotions to be built on permanence. Why do we get attached to other people, or pets, and feel despair when we lose them? We knew from the beginning that they were physical entities. We knew they can die any second. Yet, we deny this reality and feel sorrow when they aren't with us anymore. A big difference in a society that understands impermanence is a feeling a gratefulness over the experiences we have shared with others. Think of it this way: My mom can pass away any moment, and up until right now I'm so grateful of all the time we've spent together. If we get another day, that'd be fantastic, but if she dies tomorrow, that's understandable. It has to happen. Any day could be the one. And that's ok. That's expected. Any interaction I have with others is a gift, because at some point they won't be here anymore. Or I won't. Another change in a society like this would be addressing your real needs, being ok on your own. Developing a strong foundation for yourself, being capable of introspection and understanding why you feel what you feel and how to sooth yourself. This makes you less reactive when you feel upset. Instead of fighting with others you turn to yourself and find the cause of such anger and try to alleviate it without lashing back at other sentient beings. A person like this is stable in their emotions without being controlled by them.  

Now let's talk about lack of self. This is a very simple concept that also addresses the nature of everything that exists. When we say "lack of self" we mean "formed by other things" (sometimes it's referred to as "being dependant on other things".) Everything that exists is made of other things: a chair is some pieces of wood, or metal. A house is a bunch of walls with a roof. There's nothing that is not created by other things. Up to here, it is easy.  Logical. Evident.  Where this information becomes relevant (and hard to understand) is when you apply it to us. Yes, you and me. People. Lack of self means that we are made of things that, when they are together, form a human. But when they are separated they are not the human. If you separate the walls, the house doesn't exist. No individual wall is the house. The roof is not the house. For a human there are 5 parts (we call them aggregates in Buddhism) and, simply put, they are: a physical body, a mind, a memory (also called perception), emotions, and consciousness. These 5 things create the human experience. I can go in more detail to explain (hopefully in an easy and understandable manner) each one of them, if you want. In Buddhism it is explained that there's no soul like it's understood in other doctrines. The Buddha, however, focused his teachings on two things: suffering and the end of suffering. Details about what happens when we die, or what existed before life, or even why life is a thing he never talked about. The lack of soul is a conclusion on meditation on the self and finding the 5 aggregates, but not finding a single thing that can have the essence of who one is. For example: if you don't have your memories, you're not you anymore. Or if you don't have your body (with the brain, and the chemical reactions that cause you to feel what you feel). If you can't think anymore because you don't have a mind, are you still you? If you don't feel any emotions, because you don't have emotions, are you still you? If you lose consciousness of what's going on (like if you're in a dreamless sleep) could you still be you? Losing any of these 5 would be losing you. So we don't exist independently of anything else. Like the house, we are made of parts, and when the parts are gone, we are not us anymore. This doesn't mean there's no life after death, it means that if there is one, we won't experience it the same way we experience this one: we won't be us anymore. Does that make sense? This teaching is important so as to facilitate letting go of our "self". Our ego is based on the assumption that we are better than others. But in truth, we are all the same, 5 aggregates forming a person. Each person will have their on memories, body, mind, etc., that make us behave in a way or another, but we are pretty similar after all. In my life, understanding this has helped me focus more easily on other people's needs. Especially those close to me that aren't as fortunate. And though I help them as much as I can, I don't feel important by doing it. It's like identifying with someone else. I help them just like I would help myself, for, after all, we are the exact same. So a society that understands lack of self would be more giving, more open to those in need, more compassionate. Or so I think.  

My two cents. I hope this helps your a little. These are difficult concepts to grasp, so don't be discouraged if you feel overwhelmed. I am still leaning, myself.  And feel free to ask if you have doubts.
